symptoms:
En general, las reacciones adversas a la planta Dahlia pueden incluir:

- Signos digestivos: dolor abdominal, náuseas, vómitos (gravedad: leve a moderada)
- Signos dérmicos: erupciones cutáneas, picazón (gravedad: leve)
- Signos neurológicos: mareos, somnolencia (gravedad: leve)

Es importante destacar que la planta Dahlia no es tóxica y no se han reportado casos de intoxicación grave en humanos. Sin embargo, si se ingiere una gran cantidad de la planta o se entra en contacto con ella en una piel irritada, puede ocurrir una reacción adversa. Si se experimentan síntomas de intoxicación, es importante buscar atención médica.
description: La Dahlia capnobela es una planta herbácea perenne que se caracteriza por su porte erecto y ramificado. Sus hojas son ovales, enteras y de color verde oscuro, con una longitud de hasta 20 cm. Las flores son grandes y pomponiformes, con un diámetro de hasta 15 cm, y presentan un colorido variado que puede incluir tonos de rojo, naranja, amarillo y blanco. Los frutos son aquenios pequeños y no tienen un color específico. Un rasgo distintivo de la Dahlia es su capacidad para producir una gran variedad de colores y formas en sus flores, lo que la hace una planta muy apreciada en jardinería.

description: Delphinium purpusii is a rare species of larkspur known by the common names Kern County larkspur and rose-flowered larkspur. It is endemic to California where it is known only from Kern and Tulare Counties in the region where the Sierra Nevada meets the Mojave Desert. It grows on rocky cliffs and talus. This wildflower reaches between one half and one meter in height. The erect thin stem has deeply lobed leaves around the base and a small, narrow inflorescence of generally ten to 20 flowers at the top. The flowers of this species are bright pink, making it unusual among the mainly blue-flowered plants of this genus. The sepals curl either forward or back. description: Delphinium stachydeum is a species of larkspur known by the common name spiked larkspur. It is native to the Pacific Northwest and Great Basin of the United States, where it grows in sagebrush scrub and along the edges of mountain forest habitat where it meets prairie and plateau. It is a perennial herb producing at least one erect, slightly hairy stem generally exceeding a meter in height. The multilobed leaves are located mainly on the lower half of the stem except for the area just above ground level. The inflorescence is a branching array of usually more than 30 flowers, each held on a long pedicel. The flower has bright blue sepals around a centimeter long fringed with hairs and surrounding smaller, paler petals. The spur at the back of the flower is just over a centimeter in length. It is endemic to Ozark highlands in eight southwestern Missouri counties and eight counties in northwestern Arkansas.
